sources.checked_claim: Mike Cohn describes unit as the largest/base layer, UI at the top and minimized, and service testing as the middle layer covering application services separately from UI. Supports B’s broad ordering/distribution; it does not establish that all tests must run in that sequence.

§5.1.1: test plan describes objectives, resources, processes and means/schedule, helps meet criteria, and demonstrates adherence to test policy/strategy or explains deviations. §5.1.6: pyramid models differing test granularity and supports automation/effort allocation; layer number/names may differ and high-level tests are generally slower and cover broader functionality. It does not define a standalone strategy document or equate strategy with metric lists/reports.

FACTS.reason: CTFL supports the general distinction that planning describes objectives/resources/processes and adheres to policy/strategy; the supplied Q1 theory and correct option D treat strategy as justified selection/prioritization for goals, risks, constraints, and feedback. The exact standalone strategy definition is not prescribed by CTFL §5.1.1, so D is a sound contextual characterization rather than a quoted normative definition.

ANSC.reason: The visible stem asks both what a test strategy is and why it is needed. The saved table marks A, B, C, and D as covering both parts. On review, each option has a definition clause (“Стратегия — …”) and an explicit purpose clause (“она нужна …” or “она нужна для …”); all four are complete responses to both halves. Their errors lie in the proposed definition/reasoning, not in omitting a half. Wrong answers are defensible as complete misconceptions: taxonomy as rationale, metrics as strategy, and execution report as strategy.

FACTS.reason: Cohn’s page supports the common unit-base/service-middle/UI-top model, many unit checks, and minimizing UI tests. CTFL §5.1.6 independently describes granularity-based allocation and allows varying names/counts. It supports B’s distribution, but does not prescribe every option’s risk/feedback-cost decision rule as a formal pyramid definition; that application is consistent with the theory’s broader context.

ANSC.reason: The visible stem asks both what the Testing Pyramid is and how to apply it. The saved table marks all four options as covering both. Each option describes a model/distribution and follows with an application or implication: execution order and sufficiency (A), risk/cost-based allocation (B), broad-path majority (C), or dropping broader levels by code coverage (D). Thus no option omits a requested half; A/C/D fail because their proposed models/application are mistaken, not incomplete.
